newsitem.title: GUAM: S. Korean jumbo jet crashes in Guam with 254 aboard.
newsitem.headline: S. Korean jumbo jet crashes in Guam with 254 aboard.

text.p: A South Korean jumbo jet with 254 people on board crashed and burst into flames after hitting an oil pipeline on this Pacific island on Wednesday and officials said about 50 people survived.

The Korean Air Lines Boeing 747 flying mostly South Korean tourists and honeymooners from Seoul crashed down a steep slope in a rugged jungle area just miles from the airport as it prepared to land in a tropical downpour.
About 50 people survived and were being pulled from the wreckage, South Korean Transport Minister Lee Hwan-kyun said in Seoul. He expected the number of survivors to rise.
U.S. military personnel were carving a jungle path for heavy equipment to slice open the wreckage and free any survivors trapped inside, officials said.
"We have heard that there might be some additional survivors in the fuselage," said Cmdr. Kevin Wensing, a spokesman for the U.S. Pacific Fleet in Pearl Harbour.

Airline officials said there were 13 foreigners aboard, mostly Americans. There were three infants and a prominent South Korean member of parliament among the passengers, who were mostly South Koreans going on holiday, they said.
Navy helicopters had ferried at least 25 survivors to the U.S. Naval Hospital at Guam, the spokesman said. Hospital staff said survivors were being treated for severe burns and lacerations.
Airline officials said Flight 801 was carrying 231 passengers and 23 crewmembers when it crashed.
In an interview with ABC television, Guam Gov. Carl Gutierrez said a New Zealand survivor told him it was "like a normal landing" until the plane smashed into the ground.
The governor said the plane, flying from Seoul to Guam, caught fire after rupturing an oil pipeline on the ground.

Gutierrez and his wife rushed to the scene and helped pull survivors out of the wreckage, including an 11-year-old Japanese girl who begged him to rescue her mother. He could not save the woman because of the fierce flames.

The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board launched an immediate investigation into the crash, chairman Jim Hall said at a Seattle news conference. He said investigators would be looking in particular at a vital piece of airport safety equipment that was not in service for the landing.
Hall said officials on Guam had confirmed that the airport's glide slope, a device used for instrument landing during poor visibility, had been out of service for some time.
But he added that instrument landings could also be made without the glide slope and there was no immediate indication as to what caused the crash.
Eduardo Cruz, a doctor at Guam Memorial Hospital, said staff members could see the flaming wreckage from the hospital miles away.

"We didn't hear anything, but we walked out and looked up and there was a big fireball on the mountain," Cruz told KCAL TV in Los Angeles. He said the hospital was about six miles (10 km) from the crash site.
Cruz said the site of the crash was "very dense, rugged terrain" and that it had been raining "rather heavily" in the last 2-3 days.
"We believe there are 29 to 30 survivors and most have been taken to the Navy medical centre," Andrew Murphy, spokesman for the Guam Airport Authority, told Reuters by telephone.
Ginger Cruz, spokeswoman for Gutierrez, said some survivors had broken limbs and the most serious ones were immediately taken to hospitals by helicopter.
White House officials said there were unconfirmed reports that the pilot of the jumbo jet "declared an in-flight emergency because of a possible fire on board."
An FAA spokeswoman said the plane had just been cleared for landing at 2:35 a.m. local time on Wednesday (12:35 p.m. EDT on Tuesday) (1635 GMT on Tuesday) when radar contact was lost.
Air safety sources said visibility at the time was limited to about one mile (1.6 km) due to the heavy rain.
Korea Broadcasting System (KBS), quoting air controllers in Guam, said the captain of the jumbo jet said the words "Something wrong" shortly before he lost contact with them.

Korean officials said Shin Ki-ha, a four-term lawmaker and former parliamentary leader of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, his wife and about 20 party members were on the plane.

Guam, largest of the Mariana Islands in the Western Pacific, is an unincorporated territory of the United States with a population of about 144,000. A U.S. military base covers about one-third of the island, the westernmost U.S. territory, which is located 4,000 miles (6,437 km) west of Hawaii and 2,200 miles (3,540 km) south east of Seoul.
